title: The Chair of Saint Peter (22 February)
hook: a feast of Peter's teaching office, not a piece of furniture

segments.voice: Yesterday, the First Sunday of Lent: the desert, three temptations, and your line, forty days. Which pull did you notice: comfort, attention or power? Day six hundred fifty-three.

Walk to the far end of Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome, past the great canopy over the altar, and look up. Floating in a burst of gilded rays, held up by four giant bronze figures, is a chair. A huge, ornate bronze throne by the sculptor Bernini. Tourists photograph it and ask, is that where the pope sits? It isn't. And the feast on February 22 isn't really about a chair either. It's about a word that gave us cathedral.
screen: `THE FAR END OF SAINT PETER'S.` → `A FLOATING BRONZE CHAIR.` → `NOT WHERE THE POPE SITS.`

segments.voice: In the ancient world, a teacher sat to teach. The chair, in Greek and Latin cathedra, was the sign of authority to teach. A bishop's church is called a cathedral because his chair is in it. So the Chair of Saint Peter is a feast of a role, not of furniture: Peter's office of teaching and holding the Church together, which Catholics believe continues in the bishop of Rome. The gospel is Matthew 16. Jesus asks his disciples, who do people say I am? Then, who do you say I am? Simon answers: Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God. And Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "That thou art Peter; and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." It's a pun. Peter's new name, Petros in Greek, Kepha in Aramaic, means rock. Christians read this verse differently, and fairly. Catholics see here Peter's office as the rock, handed on to his successors. Orthodox Christians honor Peter as first among the apostles but understand that primacy differently. Many Protestants read the rock as Peter's confession of faith, or as Christ himself. Inside Bernini's bronze chair is an older wooden one, long honored as Peter's; scholars date it to the ninth century. The Church once kept two separate feasts of Peter's chair, one for Rome and one for Antioch, where tradition says he led the church first; they were combined on this day. And remember who got the name: the same man who would deny knowing Jesus three times. The rock was a man who cracked, and was forgiven.
screen: `A TEACHER SAT TO TEACH.` · `WHO DO YOU SAY I AM?` · `PETROS, KEPHA: ROCK.` · `ONE VERSE, READ DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `UPON THIS ROCK I WILL BUILD MY CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who carries a heavy responsibility. Catholics pray for the pope today, and if you pray, you can do that: for his health, his judgment, his peace. If you don't, choose anyone who has to hold a group together: a parent, a principal, a team lead, a pastor. Sit with what it must be like to be the rock others lean on, and to be a person who can crack. Wish them strength. The bell holds the time.
The Chair of Saint Peter. A feast on February 22 of Peter's office of teaching and unity, which Catholics believe continues in the pope. Today's word.
screen: `THE CHAIR OF SAINT PETER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: upon this rock. Today, be steady for one person who's leaning on you, even if you've cracked before. Day six hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics keep February 22 as the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, praying for the pope; in Saint Peter's Basilica the altar of the Chair is decorated with candles for the day.

notes: The wooden chair inside Bernini's Cathedra Petri (completed 1666) is dated by studies (1968–1974) to the 9th century, traditionally linked to Charles the Bald. Confirm.
Separate feasts (Chair at Rome, January 18; Chair at Antioch, February 22) were merged in the 1960 calendar reform. Confirm.
Descriptions of Orthodox and Protestant readings of Matthew 16:18 are general and unranked; confirm fairness.
The voice paraphrases Simon's answer ('Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God', Matthew 16:16 DR) without quotation marks.
